      <description><p>Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2026/nov/23/russia-ukraine-war-zelenskyy-libya-benghazi-drone-attack-ship-merkury-un-nato-europe-latest-news-updates">Europe live – latest updates</a></p></li></ul><p>Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/22/blast-russian-ship-suspected-drone-attack-benghazi-libya">strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya</a> on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.</p><p>Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/23/ukraine-naval-drones-strike-russian-warship-libya">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/california-coastal-communities-alert-big-waves-hit-state</link>
      <description><p>Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded</p><p>Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.</p><p>Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/california-coastal-communities-alert-big-waves-hit-state">Continue reading...</a></description>

</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/d7a75eea-1b1f-11f1-86b4-005056bfb2b6/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26067484115759.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/d7a75eea-1b1f-11f1-86b4-005056bfb2b6/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26067484115759.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">c1631b3e-e751-11f1-941c-6b60b041de3b</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 15:50:11 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/d7a75eea-1b1f-11f1-86b4-005056bfb2b6/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26067484115759.jpg">© Alireza Sotakbar, AP</source><dc:creator>FRANCE 24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>12,000 evacuated from Don Toliver concert after unknown substance sickens fans</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261123-12-000-evacuated-from-don-toliver-concert-after-unknown-substance-sickens-fans</link><description>
More than 12,000 fans were evacuated from a concert by American rapper Don Toliver and over 80 were treated by medics after an unknown irritant was released in the crowd, authorities in the English city of Manchester said Monday.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/1342f74c-e754-11f1-9e59-1bac47ab2f5d/w:1024/p:16x9/minimanchester.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/1342f74c-e754-11f1-9e59-1bac47ab2f5d/w:1024/p:16x9/minimanchester.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">29a5c636-e754-11f1-b238-4b6329e1cde4</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 15:46:48 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category>Down to Earth</category><title>Behind COP31 failure: A showdown over fossil fuel interests</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/down-to-earth/20261123-behind-cop31-failure-a-showdown-over-fossil-fuel-interests</link><description>
Several countries and environmental groups expressed fury at the collapse of the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey on Sunday, amid a dramatic failure to thrash out an agreement, two days after the summit was scheduled to end. Oil-producing states blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels – the root cause of the climate crisis – with the EU then refusing to back a weakened text. Our Environment Editor Valerie Dekimpe tells us more.

The final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday just landed, and it finally puts the spotlight on our boy Steve Rogers.

Avengers: Doomsday has been promising the scale and excitement the MCU has often been lacking since the Infinity Saga. Disney and Marvel Studios have just released a "final trailer" that puts the focus back on Steve Rogers — no longer Captain America but still ready to use Mjolnir — and Thor as the veterans leading the New Avengers, former colleagues, the Fantastic Four, and even Fox's X-Men (after some first-encounter fights, of course) against Doom and his followers.

A few dodgy CG shots aside, it looks grand, and if you're a big X-Men fan, it's hard not to get goosebumps when Cyclops (James Marsden) finally gets to say the thing.

The multiverse-spanning story is still largely kept a secret in this trailer, but at least we get a better sense of what the emotional stakes are for Rogers and how all these heroes can realistically work together against the greatest threat they've faced so far (even if most of them won't get more than a few lines).

As for Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom, this isn't his trailer, but the mysterious Latverian witches — who have fueled many theories online for months — are finally seen in motion.

Doom has, however, received a simple but evocative poster that mirrors one of the original Iron Man ones. Even though Marvel Studios' honcho, Kevin Feige, has shot down the theory that this Victor Von Doom is a Tony Stark variant, you can't stop marketing from doing the obvious things, it seems. ]]> <![CDATA[ The remains of a long-dead volcano on Mars | Space photo of the day for Nov. 23, 2026 ]]>

Researchers have spotted an ancient, "dead" Martian volcano from orbit around the Red Planet.

What is it?

The European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft, which has been orbiting and studying the planet since it arrived in 2003, recently captured incredible new imagery of the volcano Tharsis Tholus.

This snapshot was captured by the spacecraft's High Resolution Stereo Camera.

Even as old and worn as it is, the Martian volcano stands at around 4.97 miles (8 kilometers) tall which is comparable to some of the highest peaks in the Himalayan mountains.

Despite its impressive height, it's still only about a medium-sized volcano for Mars, which is home much more impressively-sized volcanoes. For example, the planet's largest volcano Olympus Mons measures in at roughly 13.2 miles high (21.3 kilometers).

Why is it incredible?

While Tharsis Tholus might not be the tallest volcano on Mars, it is incredibly steep. It is steeper than Mauna Kea in Hawaii on Earth. To fully showcase the volcano's structure and topography in 3D, researchers actually exaggerated the vertical scale in this image, ESA reported.

In addition to being steep and fairly tall, the volcano also has an interesting history. You can see that it is speckled with what look like small holes which are actually craters created by impacts from objects like asteroids. The volcano's current, unique shape is a combined effort by these impacts, environmental factors causing erosion and warping and ancient lava flows that left behind built-up material.

The observations by Mars Express also reveals cracks and other imperfections in the volcano. All of these details might seem like superficial bits of detail, however every small crater, every lumpy cliffside and every worn down surface hides information about the planet's past.

By studying features like volcanoes on Mars, researchers can piece together what the planet may have looked like in its ancient past. How active was this volcano? How did it interact with the landscape around it? Observations like this can hold the answers.

]]> <![CDATA[ I’m planning my first dark sky trip, and all because this educational star projector showed me what I’m missing ]]> I didn’t expect much as I unboxed the Brainstorm Night Sky; after all, I’m significantly older than this educational star projector’s target audience. Perhaps I’d come away with a sense of wonder and delight, coupled with mild irritation at having to hunt down three AA batteries to power it.

Instead, I was filled with envy as the Brainstorm Night Sky reminded me just what I was missing, thanks to the rigors of light pollution. A few minutes after powering it down, I was already making plans for my first dark sky trip, yearning for a view that rivaled the Brainstorm’s cosmic images.

Brainstorm Night Sky Projector review

Whatever your age, the Brainstorm Night Sky is so simple to use

Draw the curtains, press the Night Sky’s single button (tilting the projector and twisting the focus as appropriate) and it projects a circular image onto a ceiling or wall. Press the button again and the projection slowly begins to rotate, slowly but stutter-free. It really is that simple to operate and, aimed at budding astronomers aged eight or above, it's reasonably lightweight without feeling flimsy.

Specifications

Weight: 14.8 oz (420 g)
Bulb type: Non-specified
Laser: No
Control: On-unit
Rotation: Yes, one speed
Projection area: Up to 8.2 ft (2.5 m)
Sleep timer: Yes (30 mins)
Power: 3x AA batteries
Speaker: No

I was initially a little surprised by the size of the projection: at up to 8.2 feet (2.5 m) wide it’s not going to fill an entire ceiling. It also switches off after 30 minutes, a limit that can’t be disabled, so if you’re looking to put on your own space-themed party this is not the projector for you. But it’s on point for home education and, priced from $49.99, the Brainstorm Night Sky projector won’t break the bank.

There’s minimal distortion around the edge of the images; the planets are spherical from the word go, unlike some projectors where I’ve had to tweak them to stop Mars turning into an egg. And I never once had to crane my neck because half the solar system had been projected onto a bookcase.

This projector revealed what light pollution had taken from me

The Brainstorm Night Sky model I tested comes with four slides, each with a case to protect them from smudges and sticky fingers. You place one into the provided slide housing then insert that into the projector. There’s the moon, the solar system, and two showing the Northern Hemisphere’s night sky, as seen from Hawaii (a key location for astronomy).

I can appreciate the educational value of the first couple, even if I am still seething at Pluto being demoted back in 2006. But it was the latter pair of slides that really opened my eyes to what I could be seeing over my head.

I can spot maybe 10-20 stars from my backyard, cloud cover permitting; thanks to light pollution, that’s it. Even though the best stargazing apps can show me what I should see, when I step outside, all I typically see with the naked eye is the odd pinprick in the void.

But as soon as I inserted that third slide, a striking stellar display appeared above my head, with more stars than I could hope to count. Even knowing that Hawaii’s night sky stretches far further than eight feet across, the difference between this view and the one from my house was like night and day. Brainstorm claims this slide features over 20,000 stars, though that’s likely referring to the source photo rather than the projected image.

The fourth slide — the same crisp starscape but with every visible constellation labelled — was almost as attention-grabbing. Educational value aside, it drove home that I couldn’t see the majority of these star patterns to name them, my local night sky is that polluted.

Knowing what I was missing out on made me determined to take my stargazing further afield. Some of the best smart telescopes can lessen the impact of light pollution, but stepping away from skyglow is the most effective option. Hawaii’s a little far to travel, but I’ve already started looking into local dark sky sites. I just need to grab a pair of the best binoculars for stargazing, hop on my bike and I’m ready to go.

The Brainstorm Night Sky is a solid, budget-priced educational tool, but it has one drawback

The Brainstorm Night Sky’s projections are crisp enough that you can easily make out every constellation name, but they could be a hair brighter. The Ainael Meter Galaxy Projector, for example, delivers more illumination.

If you want to use the Brainstorm Night Sky to relax, the rotate function gives its projections an oddly hypnotic effect, and the device is whisper-quiet to boot. And while Brainstorm doesn’t specify battery life, one set of rechargeables lasted me for several days.

Unfortunately, the Brainstorm Night Sky's slide collection is a little limited. There are two models, a blue version with four slides (the one I tested) and a gray version with six slides (featuring additional space shuttle and black hole images). The included instructions state you can purchase an additional slide disc showing the Southern Hemisphere’s stars, but that’s a maximum of seven images. Nor is this projector compatible with the slides from the Brainstorm Deep Sky Projector

It’s a little disappointing given that Brainstorm has clearly put thought into the projector’s educational value. Those instructions double as a poster of the solar system, and children can use a “secret code” (printed on the instructions) to explore more astronomy facts on the company’s website.

Offering extra slide packs, of the kind you can buy for the Pococo Galaxy Projector, would give it more long-term appeal. As is, I can see its novelty and educational value diminishing over time, at which point you can upgrade to one of the best star projectors.

If you’re not bothered by the lack of expandability, the Brainstorm Night Sky’s price, image quality and ease of use still make it a useful tool for kindling a child’s interest in astronomy, or as a budget-friendly gift for junior stargazers. It’s certainly spurred me into action — how much is a plane ticket to Hawaii, anyway?

]]> <![CDATA[ What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars? ]]> On July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket. The spacecraft's mission included the study of Mars and the Martian moon Phobos, with a planned close approach and deployment of landing probes, and over the next several months, the spacecraft successfully captured more than three dozen images of Phobos during its time in service.

However, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft. Adding to the mystery were objects in some of the final photographs dispatched by the doomed spacecraft, which seemed to show an elongated shadow beneath the probe — a strange twist in one of the Soviet Union's final space missions, and one that soon gave rise to conspiracy theories about what the fate of Phobos 2 might have been.

So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure?

Last of the Soviet space explorers

Originally, the Soviet Union had planned for Phobos 2 to reach the Red Planet by late January 1989, after which the spacecraft would begin collecting data about the Martian environment leading up to its initial contact with Mars' largest moon in early June.

To say that a lot hinged on the success of the mission would be an understatement, given the unfortunate fate of the probe's predecessor, Phobos 1, which went offline on Sept. 2, 1988, after a faulty command sequence was initiated while the spacecraft was on its way to Mars. The stakes were almost immediately raised as Phobos 2 arrived in orbit around Mars on Jan. 30, 1989, when one of the probe's three onboard flight system processors was found to have gone offline, with another already experiencing technical issues.

Over the course of the next several weeks, Phobos 2 was able to overcome some of these setbacks and successfully began sending useful scientific data about the Martian environment back to Earth. By March, all the probe's science instruments appeared to be functioning normally, and despite the earlier loss of one of its processors, the remaining two had continued to facilitate control of the spacecraft by its Soviet ground control team.

Unexplained failure

That all changed on March 27, 1989, as Phobos 2 prepared to capture navigational images of its namesake as the Martian moon passed, which would be useful in advance of another forthcoming flyby in early April.

Achieving this meant that the probe had to be angled in such a way that it faced Phobos, whereby its communications antennas would be temporarily directed away from Earth. During the imaging portion of the maneuver, all appeared to go smoothly, but soon afterward, ground controllers realized they were unable to reestablish contact with the probe.

A few fleeting radio contacts were made over the ensuing hours, which engineers believed might indicate that during the period of signal loss required for imagery of Phobos to be obtained, the spacecraft may have begun to spin uncontrollably. If this were the case, and the spacecraft could not reorient its solar panels toward the sun, it would eventually lose all power.

No further contact with Phobos 2 could be established beyond this point, although images from the probe's final close encounter with the Martian moon were successfully delivered back to Soviet ground controllers. While investigators identified a failure involving the spacecraft's onboard computer system as the most probable explanation, to this day, the exact cause of the events leading to the loss remains unknown.

Theories involving the failure

Although questions remain about the fate of Phobos 2, several theories have been put forward over the years. According to authors Paolo Ulivi and David M. Harland, one of the simplest explanations was that the spacecraft was damaged after an impact with other material orbiting the Martian moon, although later modeling by Soviet engineers and American teams at NASA's Jet Propulsion Lab seemed to rule this out.

A more likely scenario involved failure of the probe's second attitude control computer, which had already begun experiencing technical issues as Phobos 2 arrived in Martian orbit. With two of its three processors now offline, the third and sole remaining computer was unable to maintain control of the spacecraft on its own. An additional factor might have been power loss from battery drainage while the probe's solar arrays were directed away from the sun, and with no failsafe to power down any non-critical systems under such conditions, the spacecraft would likely have undergone significant power loss.

However, the probe's failure was only one part of the mystery: equally perplexing had been the unusual images Phobos 2 captured in its final moments, which later sparked speculation — and conspiracy theories — about what might have been behind the spacecraft's sudden demise.

The shadow in Phobos 2's final photos

In some of the final images captured by Phobos 2, an unusual, elongated shadow had been visible in the frame, which with time would begin to prompt the most unusual of all the theories about the probe's demise: that it had been disabled by an alien spacecraft.

Among the proponents of this theory had been Marina Popovich, a former experimental pilot and the first Soviet woman to break the sound barrier, who set over 100 world aviation records in her career. In 1991, Popovich held a press conference at the Soviet Consulate in San Francisco, where she claimed a cigar-shaped object had been photographed near the Martian moon, which she believed to be an alien mothership.

Given her storied background in Soviet aerospace history, Popovich's views likely carried a degree of credibility unlike most others. However, that did not make them accurate.

Explaining the Phobos "shadow"

Determining what the images actually show requires an understanding of the probe's orbit, particularly with relation to the Martian moon it was attempting to photograph. At the time, the spacecraft and Phobos were in almost the same orbit, and moving at very similar speeds. As Ulivi and Harland note, due to these conditions, the probe's Termoskan multispectral imager often captured images that "included the shadow of the moon on the planet's surface as a dark oblong cigar-shaped feature."

In 1991, a NASA-led study of the Termoskan observations concluded that the unusual appearance of the shadow most likely resulted from a combination of factors acting together. The study team attributed these to the scanning instrument itself, as well as the spacecraft's near-co-orbital motion with Phobos, its viewing direction, and finally, a slight rocking motion the researchers concluded the spacecraft had likely exhibited at the time.

However, another factor that contributed to the appearance of the shadow involves the oblique angle at which the moon's shadow strikes the Martian surface. Because of this, similar imagery depicting an elliptical or elongated shadow cast by Phobos has been obtained since the Phobos 2 mission, with examples including images captured by the High-Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC) on the ESA's Mars Express spacecraft in 2005.

The legacy of the Soviet Phobos missions

The loss of Phobos 2 became a controversy for reasons other than the imaginative speculations about what its final images might have captured.

John M. Logsdon, director of the Space Policy Institute at George Washington University's School of International Affairs, remarked to the Los Angeles Times shortly after the failure that the situation was "just horrible," noting that the mishap was expected to potentially fuel what he called "a first-rate bureaucratic struggle" the Soviet Union was undergoing amid political changes occurring there at the time.

As it begins to run low on hydrogen for nuclear fusion reactions in its core, the star's energy generation begins to falter and its interior starts to contract under gravity. This has the effect of raising the temperature throughout the star, causing an outer shell of hydrogen to ignite its own fusion reactions. The star promptly bloats to become a red giant tens or even hundreds of millions of kilometers across.

Soon enough the star ceases fusion reactions completely. The star's outer layers are shed and they expand out into space, while its core contracts to become an inert white dwarf with a diameter similar to Earth but with a mass generally between half and two-thirds of a solar mass.

Amazon's first satellite launch since a rocket failure doomed 40 of its spacecraft is set for Tuesday morning (Nov. 24), and you can watch the action live.

An Ariane 6 rocket carrying 36 satellites for the Amazon Leo constellation is scheduled to lift off from Europe's Spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana, on Tuesday (Nov. 23), during a 29-minute window that opens at 5:45 a.m. EST (1045 GMT; 7:45 a.m. local time in Kourou). You can watch it live here at Space.com courtesy of Arianespace, the French company that operates the Ariane 6.

The launch was originally supposed to take place on Monday (Nov. 23), but that attempt was scrubbed due to a technical issue affecting the rocket's ground support systems, according to Arianespace.

Amazon Leo, so named because it will operate in low Earth orbit, will compete with SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation, which currently consists of more than 11,000 operational spacecraft.

Amazon's network will eventually have more than 3,200 satellites, but just 400 or so have reached orbit to date. Another 40 were supposed to be delivered on Nov. 15, but they were lost after their rocket ride, a United Launch Alliance (ULA) Vulcan Centaur, suffered a problem shortly after launch.

Ariane 6 and Vulcan Centaur aren't the only rockets Amazon is depending on to build its broadband constellation. Jeff Bezos' company has also booked rides on ULA's Atlas V rocket, Blue Origin's New Glenn and SpaceX's Falcon 9.

Vulcan will be grounded for a while as ULA investigates the Nov. 15 failure and works to fix whatever caused it. And New Glenn hasn't flown since April, when the rocket failed to deliver AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird 7 satellite to the proper orbit. New Glenn's return to flight was further complicated on May 28, when the rocket exploded during a routine prelaunch test.

The Ariane 6, the successor to Arianespace's Ariane 5 heavy lifter, debuted in July 2024 and has nine launches under its belt to date. All of them have been successful except that maiden mission, which was a partial failure.

The upcoming mission will be the fourth Amazon Leo flight for the Ariane 6, following launches in February, April and June of this year.

SpaceX set a new record with its latest satellite launch out of California.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Launch Complex-4E on Sunday (Nov. 22) at 7:23 a.m. ET (1223 GMT; 4:23 a.m. local time in California), on a mission for the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) called NROL-136.

It was the second launch from that pad in a little over 32 hours, after the USSF-317 mission for the U.S. Space Force. And that quick turnaround made history.

"Massive high five to the @SpaceX west coast team for a world record launch to launch turn from Pad 4e last night! 32 hr, 3 min, 21 sec! This smashed the previous record of 45 hrs from Pad 40. Team got there with several hours of margin. Next goal… the 24 hr turn!" Kiko Dontchev, SpaceX's vice president of launch, said via X on Sunday. (Pad 40 is at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.)

NROL-136 was the sixth launch of 2026 so far for the NRO. All of them have been carried out by SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9, and all have delivered classified satellites to low Earth orbit.

The launch marked another step in the NRO's effort to expand its intelligence-gathering capabilities through a proliferated network of spacecraft designed to provide more frequent and timely surveillance of locations around the globe.

About two minutes after liftoff, the Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued carrying the classified payloads onward to orbit. The booster then reversed course and returned to Vandenberg, touching down at Landing Zone 4 approximately seven and a half minutes after launch.

Saturday's launch was the 14th flight for this particular Falcon 9 booster, dubbed B1097, which previously launched NASA's Sentinel-6B ocean-monitoring satellite, NROL-172, USSF-259 for the Space Force, and eight Starlink missions.

NROL-136 was the 15th launch dedicated to building the NRO's "proliferated architecture," the satellites for which have been developed in partnership with SpaceX and Northrop Grumman. The network is designed to increase coverage and improve the "capability and resilience" of U.S. intelligence operations in space, according to the NRO's mission website.

The NRO began deploying the constellation in May 2024 with the launch of NROL-146. The most recent proliferated architecture mission before Sunday was NROL-179, which lifted off on June 19, 2026.

As with any classified mission, the agency has not disclosed the exact number of satellites aboard NROL-136 or revealed details about their onboard technologies.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 11 p.m. ET on Nov. 22 with the news that NROL-136 set a new record for the shortest time between two launches from the same pad.

]]> <![CDATA[ This viral star projector has been hyped to Mars and back, but we hunted down the best version you can buy ]]> It was only a matter of time, but AI has come for astronomy accessories. I’ve yet to see a fictional elderly craftsman begging you to buy his hand-carved telescopes; however, it has absolutely muddied the waters around this viral gooseneck Galaxy Projector Night Light.

The good news is that there is an impressive little star projector to be had here, and I’m here to cut through the AI-assisted hype. To make sure you’re not hoodwinked, I’ve done the online legwork to bring you the best version of this device, and it won’t cost you a fortune to put a planetarium in your pocket.

Before we dive into what makes this Galaxy Projector Night Light so great, there are a couple of pressing issues to address. No variant of this USB-powered star projector will break up heated dinner arguments by casting a beautifully animated space whale on the ceiling, as one ridiculous AI-generated advert asserts. Its projections are eye-catching enough to entertain space fans young and old, but they’re strictly static.

Also, while you might be tempted by the lure of 24 interchangeable slides, compared to this Galaxy Projector Night Light’s 13, this lesser model’s slide selection is a letdown. Not only are the slides smaller and blurrier than this model, a large number are dedicated to seasonal holidays. As much as I enjoy Christmas, if I had Santa’s colossal face gazing down at me from the ceiling I’d never sleep again.

Zanbix 2 in 1 Galaxy Projector Night Light review

More than meets the eye

I tempered my expectations when I first got my hands on the Galaxy Projector Night Light. Packed in a small, relatively unassuming box, it looks remarkably similar to the standard model that’s spread across TikTok, YouTube, Facebook and so on. Just like that one, it’s powered via USB, with a flexible stalk, a slot for slides and a nose-mounted focus wheel.

However, once I hooked it up to a handy USB socket, all my reservations vanished, and I was seriously impressed by the power of this little projector. You’ll need a darkened room but the Galaxy Projector Night Light’s larger lens is a serious step-up from the run-of-the-mill version. Its images are richer and clearer than you’d expect from a projector this size, and easily capable of transforming a mid-sized ceiling or wall into a cosmic display.

This stunning James Webb Space Telescope image of the Pillars of Creation, with its vast columns of gas and dust, is a perfect example of the projections on offer. The fact the display was static didn’t diminish its wow factor, and I spent a good 15 minutes gazing at it in wonder.

The Galaxy Projector Night Light does have a four-hour shut-off in case you drift off or want to use it to lull a child to sleep (and 12 hours for its night light function). It’s easy to adjust thanks to its flexible neck, and while it never once came loose, you’ll find some USB ports have a tighter grip than others.

Slide selection

Once I set aside the images of Santa Claus (you’re staying in the box, Saint Nick), jellyfish and a T. rex, I was left with 10 astronomy-related slides. Several, such as the black hole, are artistic illustrations, while others, like the aforementioned Pillars, are actual astronomical images.

They all have their own distinct appeal. I wouldn’t, for example, describe the black hole slide as relaxing, but it’s absolutely captivating in a cosmic horror way. I’d have appreciated an auto-rotate option, but that would have added some bulk to the projector.

Switching slides is a breeze, each image mounted in its own slide holder. Oddly, a couple of mine had hair-like marks, but those disappeared when I brought the image into focus via the nose wheel.

The full 13-slide set is:

• Angel and stars (B&W)
• Black hole
• Earth and moon
• Jellyfish
• Magellanic Cloud
• Milky Way
• Moon and stars (B&W)
• Pillars of Creation
• Santa
• Solar system
• Starfield (B&W)
• T. rex
• Whale and stars (B&W)

It’s mildly disappointing that there aren’t extra slide packs out there, but the selection is ample for entertainment, relaxation and even education. What better way to spark an interest in STEM than with the wonders of space?

Portable projection

The Galaxy Projector Night Light will run off any USB port: a laptop, desktop, charger and so on. I even got it working with my TV’s USB socket, but the real bonus was realizing I could run it off the best power banks. If you’re on the move, slip the projector and slides into one pocket, a powerbank into another, and you’re good to go for hours.

Some of the best star projectors are styled so they blend in with a room, but this one is so small you can just pack it away until you need it. The projector’s marketing even advertises it for use in the car, which seems like an accident waiting to happen. Only the Blisslights Starport is smaller, but then you’re limited to laser-dot stars.

There’s no remote and no sound options, but the Galaxy Projector Night Light is so easy to use that children should be able to get to grips with it. Literally, in fact, since while the light portion warms up, it never really gets hot. Factor in its small size and pocket-friendly price, and it’s an ideal space gift or stocking stuffer for a young stargazer.

As long as you don’t buy the hype and think you’re getting something that’ll bathe a room in beautifully animated starscapes, as several Amazon purchasers did, you’ll find this Galaxy Projector Night Light is a surprisingly capable little star projector.

Are there bigger and better models out there? Yes, and we’ve rounded up the best star projectors if this one isn’t for you. But for convenience, value for money and portability, this Galaxy Projector Night Light is a great way to bring the cosmos into your home and it’s fast cemented itself as one of my favorites.

]]> <![CDATA[ As 'Star Trek: First Contact' turns 30, Director Jonathan Frakes reflects on his triumphant time-travel blockbuster (interview) ]]> "Star Trek: First Contact" celebrates its 30th anniversary today, and the engaging sci-fi classic still looks fantastic three decades later. With the sad passing of its star, Patrick Stewart, last month, and "Star Trek's" milestone 60th birthday taking place in 2026, this is a bittersweet salute that also holds an extra special significance.

Directed by "The Next Generation's" Number One, Jonathan Frakes, in his feature film debut, "First Contact" consistently ranks as one of the finest "Star Trek" feature films among fans and critics, and those accolades are well deserved.

Based on a compelling screenplay by Brannon Braga and Ronald D. Moore, "First Contact" remains as bright and beautiful as ever, brimming with bravado, heart, horror, and heroism.

Not only was it a bona fide crowdpleaser when it was released by Paramount over Thanksgiving week on Nov. 22, 1996, but it was also a financial success for the studio, eventually pulling in a worldwide total of $212 million off a modest $45 million budget.

Honestly, who can forget Alice Krige's seductive Borg Queen, Marina Sirtis’ Deana Troi tipsy on tequila, Brent Spiner's Data feeling the sensation of human skin, Patrick Stewart’s Jean-Luc Picard reliving past traumas, and James Cromwell's Zephram Cochrane blasting off in the Phoenix and dancing to Roy Orbison's "Ooby Dooby"?

We caught up with Frakes for "First Contact's" 30th anniversary to hear why this "Trek" treasure holds up and warp back to Hollywood’s heyday of the '90s. Resistance is futile!

"What’s not to love?" Frakes tells SPACE regarding the film’s lasting popularity. "It was bulletproof. Dean Devlin ["Stargate," "Independence Day"] and I have very similar sensibilities about filmmaking. We like the whole idea of action, adventure, comedy, and in the case of 'First Contact,' a little horror as well. ILM’s John Knoll, the guy who won the Oscar for 'Star Wars,' just happened to be our Special Effects Supervisor."

"First Contact" is filled with memorable moments and indelible performances, some of which certainly stand out for Frakes looking back over the years on the production.

"The two things that always come to mind were the beautiful scene with Alfre [Woodard] and Patrick, the Moby Dick scene, where she says, 'You broke your little ships,'" he recalls. "I was sitting under the camera with my face in my hands, watching two heavyweights go at it take after take. It was what you dream of. They were into it. The writing was great. We had time to do it right, and they were fabulous together.

"That and the Cromwell and Marina drunk on tequila scene. It's not only one extended take, but it contributes to the pace of the movie in the right kind of way. My wife tells me that I was really good in that scene because I was exhausted and relaxed. It’s true, you’re exhausted when you’re filming and acting at the same time. I got to sit there and watch those two. It was like watching a tennis game."

Many Trekkies might not know that Alfre Woodard is Frakes' godmother, and he had specifically asked producer Rick Berman for approval to include her in the movie’s cast.

"She's one of our finest American actors," he notes. "Rick said, 'If we can get Alfre, that would be great.' I knew she’d do great with Patrick, so that was a no-brainer. I never had a godmother, and when I came out here to live in LA back in 1979, an old friend from college, Nathan Cook, was working with Alfre. We were at a barbecue, and it came up. She said, 'You don’t have a godmother? I’ll be your godmother.' I asked what that meant, and she said, 'I’ll be in charge of your spiritual being.' It's been a magical friendship that turned into her playing that part."

The hive-minded cybernetic collective known as the Borg featured prominently in the time-travel tale, and that second filming unit did a masterful job lighting those scenes.

"The Borg costumes were torture, from what I was told," says Frakes. "We had our own set of ADs and an entirely separate special effects makeup crew, and the costume department had a certain number of Borg to build and rebuild. Now the Borg had been on the show, but with these Borg we had more time and more moving parts. It was kind of an enhanced thing that really paid off. I look back so fondly on that entire experience. Also, the Borg were one of the great movie villains. They held up!"

Frakes couldn’t be prouder of "First Contact", and he reminds us that most people like it right next to 1982's "Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan." That's rarefied air indeed!

"We got Cromwell coming off of 'Babe.' So we had Alfre and Alice and Cromwell. They joined our family effortlessly. Because we'd done seven TV seasons, 182 episodes, and a movie already together, we were thick as thieves and still are; may Patrick rest in peace. The three of them joined us as if we’d been dancing with them forever."

"Star Trek: First Contact" is available to stream on Paramount+.

 <description>Kvůli plánované výstavbě nového obchvatu Pardubic z Dražkovic do Černé za Bory musí proběhnout likvidace staré ekologické zátěže. Lhůta pro podávání nabídek vyprší 1. prosince.</description>

 <description>V Týništi nad Orlicí skončí v noci po více než roce a půl dopravní komplikace. O půlnoci z pondělí na úterý se pro řidiče znovu otevřou mosty ve směru na Albrechtice.  <description>Plynaři v Plzeňském kraji, stejně jako v celém Česku, zkontrolují před zimou těsnost rozvodů zesíleným zápachem.  <description>Soukromý investor plánuje v Lokti na Sokolovsku otevřít muzeum historických motorek.  <description>Stát by měl jen doporučovat, co mají školní jídelny vařit, myslí si 47 % Čechů. Dle průzkumu agentury Median pro Radiožurnál naopak 40 % Čechů podporuje závazné standardy. Vláda v listopadu rozhodla, že vyhláška o školním stravování nebude povinná.  <description>Místo úlevy další týden dopravních komplikací. Dělníci a jejich zaměstnavatelé nestihli včas dokončit opravu Pisáreckého tunelu v Brně.  <description>V petrochemickém závodu v Novošachtinsku na jihozápadě Ruska vypukl po tříhodinovém náletu ukrajinských dronů rozsáhlý požár. Podle očitých svědků hoří jedna ze skladovacích nádrží. Jasná záře na obloze je vidět desítky kilometrů daleko, napsal ruský server Kuzbass-segodnja. V Novošachtinsku podle portálu Donpress.ru hoří nejen rafinerie, ale i areál společnosti Tata-gaz, kde jsou sklady pohonných hmot. Ruské úřady se dosud nevyjádřily.</description>

Nárazová odorizace probíhá každoročně před vrcholem topné sezony a zásadním způsobem přispívá k bezpečnému provozu plynárenských zařízení.</description></item><item><title>Vánoční strom na Staromáku pochází z Liberce. Ozdobí jej obří světelná mašle</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906453-vanocni-strom-na-staromaku-ozdobi-obri-svetelna-masle-novinka-poslouzi-i-jako-fotokoutek.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906453-vanocni-strom-na-staromaku-ozdobi-obri-svetelna-masle-novinka-poslouzi-i-jako-fotokoutek.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 14:55:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Barbora Genser</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Praha už zná podobu letošního vánočního stromu na Staroměstském náměstí. Smrk z libereckých Šimonovic byl v sobotu pokácen a zamířil na cestu do centra metropole. Největší novinkou letošní výzdoby bude čtyřmetrová 3D světelná mašle, která zároveň poslouží jako netradiční fotokoutek.</description></item><item><title>Liberečtí šermíři byli 81 let bez zázemí. Teď vybírají na svůj první sál</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906479-liberecti-sermiri-byli-81-let-bez-zazemi-ted-vybiraji-na-svuj-prvni-sal.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906479-liberecti-sermiri-byli-81-let-bez-zazemi-ted-vybiraji-na-svuj-prvni-sal.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 12:40:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Vychovávají mládežnické reprezentanty, přesto už osm desetiletí jen kočují po pronájmech. Šerm Liberec, z. s. konečně staví vlastní zázemí v Truhlářské ulici v Liberci, které bude dětem otevřené nonstop. S vybavením nového sálu teď můžete oddílu pomoct ve sbírce na Donio.cz.</description></item><item><title>Promenádní cestu u přehrady v Liberci otevře město nejdřív v prosinci</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906452-promenadni-cestu-u-prehrady-v-liberci-otevre-mesto-nejdriv-v-prosinci.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906452-promenadni-cestu-u-prehrady-v-liberci-otevre-mesto-nejdriv-v-prosinci.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 11:20:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Oblíbenou promenádní cestu u přehrady v Liberci otevře město nejdřív v prosinci. Práce mají několikaměsíční zpoždění a město za úpravu okolí vodního díla zaplatí bezmála 90 milionů korun. Původně radnice počítala s částkou pod 80 milionů.</description></item><item><title>Poděkování fanouškům, absolutorium hráčům. Trenér Fodrek byl po Spartě spokojený</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/fotbal/906461-podekovani-fanouskum-absolutorium-hracum-trener-fodrek-byl-po-sparte-spokojeny.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/fotbal/906461-podekovani-fanouskum-absolutorium-hracum-trener-fodrek-byl-po-sparte-spokojeny.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 09:55:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Luboš Vrabec</dc:creator><category>Fotbal</category><description>Ani po výhře 3:1 na Spartě u trenéra Slovanu Branislava Fodreka nebyl vidět úsměv. Z jeho slov ale plynulo, že byl hodně spokojený, hráče chválil a děkoval i početné výpravě hostujících fanoušků. Sám ale mluvil o tom, že jeho tým na podzim čekají ještě čtyři další těžké zápasy.</description></item><item><title>V Libereckém kraji nasněžilo, silničáři radí opatrnost</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906448-v-libereckem-kraji-nasnezilo-a-misty-stale-snezi-silnicari-radi-opatrnost.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906448-v-libereckem-kraji-nasnezilo-a-misty-stale-snezi-silnicari-radi-opatrnost.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 08:33:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>V Libereckém kraji do rána nasněžilo a místy se stále objevují sněhové přeháňky, silnice jsou s opatrností sjízdné. Hlavní tahy jsou většinou jen holé a mokré, pozor by si měli dát řidiči v horských oblastech, kde může na silnicích ležet rozbředlý sníh.</description></item><item><title>Někdo ho vyhodil jako odpad. Malé kotě Bambi zachránila z kontejneru všímavá žena</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906414-nekdo-ho-vyhodil-jako-odpad-male-kote-bambi-zachranila-z-kontejneru-vsimava-zena.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906414-nekdo-ho-vyhodil-jako-odpad-male-kote-bambi-zachranila-z-kontejneru-vsimava-zena.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 06:30:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Tiché mňoukání z téměř prázdného kontejneru zachránilo v České Lípě život malému kotěti. Na pomoc zvířeti, které tam s největší pravděpodobností někdo úmyslně odložil, zavolala kolemjdoucí žena strážníky. Kočičí holčička Bambi nyní bojuje se zdravotními potížemi v útulku.</description></item><item><title>Sparta ve výročním zápase překvapivě prohrála s Libercem 1:3</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/fotbal/906433-sparta-ve-vyrocnim-zapase-prekvapive-prohrala-s-libercem-1-3.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/fotbal/906433-sparta-ve-vyrocnim-zapase-prekvapive-prohrala-s-libercem-1-3.html</guid><pubDate>Sun, 22 Nov 2026 20:09:16 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Fotbal</category><description>Fotbalisté Sparty v 15. kole první ligy ve výročním zápase překvapivě prohráli doma s Libercem 1:3 a v neúplné tabulce na čtvrté příčce ztrácejí na druhý Slovan již pět bodů. Severočeši zaostávají za vedoucí Slavií o osm bodů a k dobru mají dohrávaný duel s Ostravou.</description></item><item><title>Liberec čtyřmi góly ve druhé třetině otočil duel s Mladou Boleslaví a vyhrál 5:2</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/hokej/906431-liberec-ctyrmi-goly-ve-druhe-tretine-otocil-duel-s-mladou-boleslavi-a-vyhral-5-2.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/hokej/906431-liberec-ctyrmi-goly-ve-druhe-tretine-otocil-duel-s-mladou-boleslavi-a-vyhral-5-2.html</guid><pubDate>Sun, 22 Nov 2026 19:45:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Hokej</category><description>Hokejisté Liberce porazili ve 21. kole extraligy na svém ledě Mladou Boleslav 5:2. Před svými diváky uspěli Bílí Tygři posedmé za sebou, derby ovládli počtvrté v řadě. Bruslaři si připsali pátou prohru z posledních šesti startů, přestože po první třetině vedli.</description></item><item><title>České domácnosti dluží přes 4,5 bilionu, spotřebitelský dluh roste rekordním tempem</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906313-ceske-domacnosti-dluzi-pres-4-5-bilionu-spotrebitelsky-dluh-roste-rekordnim-tempem.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906313-ceske-domacnosti-dluzi-pres-4-5-bilionu-spotrebitelsky-dluh-roste-rekordnim-tempem.html</guid><pubDate>Sun, 22 Nov 2026 15:30:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Miroslav Adamec</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Podle údajů společnosti Czech Banking Credit Bureau (CBCB) dosáhlo celkové zadlužení obyvatel České republiky evidované v Bankovním a Nebankovním registru klientských informací na konci třetího čtvrtletí 2026 výše 4,53 bilionu korun.</description></item></channel></rss>
